title: The surface spits now, and that part is real water
question: Does the surface read as alive? And the LARGE mix — two sizes rather than a grid of identical discs — is that closer?
context_md:
Your four points, in order.

**"Both should cause a surface disturbance."** Done, and deliberately not in the renderer. Water within fifteen degrees of boiling now throws the odd real drop off its own free surface: it hops, and it falls back. It is the same code a boulder's crown uses, so the pool is actually debited and nothing is invented — and it happens with the bubbles switched **off**, which is what "both" has to mean. Watch the specks above the water in either clip.

**"How much is this still connected to the physics of the scene vs is just an animation?"** Straight answer: **the bubbles are an animation.** They are computed from position, the frame number and that cell's own temperature, with no memory and no writes back into the world — they move nothing. They are keyed to something real (water that genuinely is near boiling, and boiling that genuinely follows), but a bubble is a mark on the screen. That is exactly why I put the surface disturbance in the simulation rather than next to them: it is the one part of this that is water going somewhere.

**"Large should include a mix of this plus 1 pixel smaller bubbles."** Two sizes now, picked per site by a hash independent of the one deciding whether a site lights at all — otherwise size and presence correlate and all the small ones turn up together.

**"I want both to remain options I can A/B test in live play."** They do. `H` cycles OFF, RISING, LARGE, COLUMNS, SURFACE, and the status line names whichever is on.

Three things this cost, all found by looking rather than by a test: the first version fired **zero** times, because a pan is heated from below and its surface is the *coolest* part, so "a hot cell with air above it" describes nothing; then it fired and threw nothing, because a settled pool's top row is never quite full and the splash code will only take a full cell; then it looked like rain, because a boulder's crown is three cells thrown hard and a pan spitting is one drop that barely clears the water.

Costs nothing measurable — worst frame with the pops off and on is 8.04 against 8.60 ms on this pan.

Both clips are the same pan at true speed, zoomed 6x.

items.label: bubbles off
items.caption: No bubbles drawn at all. The surface still spits, because that part is not drawn.

items.label: large
items.caption: Two disc sizes mixed, plus the same real spitting.
